title: Taught to the sun, told again
hookLine: the sun, a king, his son, and a teaching handed down until it was lost
carry: whenever dharma declines, god comes again

cards: Three names at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu.
Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, over a long stretch of time, Krishna says, it was lost.
That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield.

teach.b: The Gita's word for this handing on is parampara: one after another, teacher to student. And Krishna tells Arjuna why it's coming to him: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret.
Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago.
How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter.

teach.h: MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.
teach.b: Many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't.
Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and Lord of all beings, he comes into being through his own power, his own maya.
And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet.
This is the teaching behind every avatar story Hindus tell, Rama, Krishna, the fish, the man-lion.
The word avatara, a coming down, isn't in these verses, but these are the verses people quote for it. And here's the link to our word.

teach.h: HIS BIRTH AND KARMA ARE DIVINE.
teach.b: In the next verse, Krishna calls his birth and his action, his karma, divine. Whoever truly knows them isn't born again on leaving the body, but comes to him.
So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting: taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently.

Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will, not forced on him by karma, as ours are.

how: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

o: the yoga of action, handed down and renewed by Krishna
a debt each king owes to the sun god himself
a curse that passes from a father to his sons

games.q: Gita, chapter four, the opening — tap the pairs.
p: the sun, first to hear the yoga
told it to his son Ikshvaku
one after another, teacher to student

s: Krishna says the yoga of action is new, taught for the first time to Arjuna
he says he taught it to the sun, it was handed down, then lost, and he's telling it again.
Arjuna objects that Krishna was born after the sun
and Krishna answers that many births have passed, for both of them.
Shankara and Ramanuja read Krishna's births the same way
Shankara speaks of an appearance by his own maya; Ramanuja insists the births are real and freely chosen.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your friend says he taught this yoga to the sun, long ago. what do you say?
o: that's impossible. you were born recently, and the sun long ago.
nothing. it's not polite to question a teacher.
games.why: Arjuna objects. Krishna answers: many births have passed for me and for you; I know them all, you don't.

practice: Bring to mind one thing someone taught you, a recipe, a prayer, a knot, how to apologize, and picture the person who taught you, then, if you can, the person who taught them.
Let the chain run back as far as you can see, into people you'll never know, and sit with the whole line behind one small skill. If you pray, you can give thanks for the whole chain.

wordCard.voice: Karma. In chapter four, a yoga of action handed down teacher to student, lost, and told again by one whose own birth and action are divine.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: parampara, one after another, the chain of teachers. Gita 4.2.

carryVoice: Your line: whenever dharma declines, God comes again. Tomorrow, a verse some families say before eating. Until then.
